paragraphs.text: Annular epidermolytic ichthyosis is a rare phenotypic variant of bullous congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma (epidermolytic ichthyosis). Affected individuals have bullous ichthyosis in early childhood, followed later by hyperkeratotic lichenified plaques on the flexural areas and extensor surfaces. They also have intermittent bouts of annular and polycyclic, erythematous, scaly plaques on the trunk and proximal extremities. Histologic examination shows epidermolytic hyperkeratosis (Joh et al., 1997; Suga et al., 1998; Mikilita et al., 2020).

paragraphs.text: Sahn et al. (1992) reported a 30-year-old white woman who developed bullous and ichthyosiform skin lesions at 8 months of age. The blistering stopped at puberty, but the hyperkeratotic plaques persisted. Two of her 5 children were affected with a bullous type of ichthyosis. At 27 years of age she developed many annular and polycyclic, erythematous, hyperkeratotic plaques on the trunk and extremities. These plaques were pruritic, enlarged slowly, and then resolved. Histopathologic examination of the annular plaques showed epidermolytic hyperkeratosis. On electron microscopy, the annular plaques showed interrupted perinuclear tonofilament rings, consistent with either bullous ichthyotic erythroderma of Brocq or ichthyosis bullosa of Siemens.

paragraphs.text: Joh et al. (1997) reported a second family with annular epidermolytic ichthyosis, with affected members in 2 generations. The proband had bullous ichthyosis and bouts of disease activity in which many annular and polycyclic, erythematous, hyperkeratotic plaques developed on the trunk and proximal extremities. Histologic examination showed the typical pathology of epidermolytic hyperkeratosis. Ultrastructural analysis showed abnormal keratin filament networks and clumping of tonofilaments in a perinuclear distribution.

paragraphs.text: Mikilita et al. (2020) reported an 8-year-old girl with diffuse dermatosis that began in the first months of life. There was no family history of similar cases and no consanguinity. She had erythematous, scaly, hyperkeratotic plaques with prominent borders. These involved the mesogastrium, cubital and popliteal fossae, and the inguinal and cervical regions. She also had palmoplantar hyperkeratosis and yellowish hyperkeratotic plaques on the scalp and nasal introitus. Hair, nails, and mucosa were unaffected, and she reported no symptoms. One month later the plaques had changed in appearance: the affected areas were more extensive, but the polycyclic aspect had disappeared. The initial diagnosis was erythrokeratodermia variabilis et progressiva. A skin biopsy from the extensor forearm showed acanthosis, papillomatosis, and hyperkeratosis with marked epidermolysis in the granular layer, which led to the diagnosis of annular epidermolytic ichthyosis. In a review of the literature in English, Portuguese, and Spanish, Mikilita et al. (2020) found 19 cases in 10 publications. Some patients had no lesions at birth, and palmoplantar keratoderma was reported in some cases but not in others.

paragraphs.text: Mikilita et al. (2020) noted that the main differential diagnosis of annular epidermolytic ichthyosis is erythrokeratodermia variabilis et progressiva (EKVP). Features that distinguish EKVP include onset during childhood, no epidermal fragility, and no epidermolysis on histology. The main ultrastructural feature of EKVP is a reduced number of keratinosomes in the granular layer.
